title: Media industry could be forced by government to improve safeguards after David Walliams allegations
description: The government is prepared to force the entertainment industry to improve safeguarding practices unless rapid change is introduced, BBC Newsnight has
body: The government is prepared to force the entertainment industry to improve safeguarding practices unless rapid change is introduced, BBC Newsnight has learned.Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy told the House of Commons she will meet representatives from the media, entertainment and sport next week to "discuss the action that we need to take" following recent allegations."But if those protections are insufficient, the government will not hesitate to take further action," she said.She could force participation in creative industries industry standards body CIISA, which is currently voluntary, to protect whistleblowers, the BBC understands.Her comments come after an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News alleged that entertainer David Walliams had been accused by several women of sexual misconduct and abusing his position, which he denies.Nandy added: "For too long, too many people have had to choose between their career and their safety. "Whistleblowers must be protected, and those who abuse their position must no longer be able to hide."Earlier this week, she said she was summoning leaders from the broadcasting, publishing, film and entertainment industries to "draw a line" in the sand.That announcement came after the publication of allegations against Walliams, as well as the sentencing of disgraced entertainer Russell Brand on charges of rape and sexual assault.The allegations against Walliams were made as a part of a joint three-year investigation that was published after the entertainer lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public. Walliams denies all the allegations against him.BBC Newsnight understands that the culture secretary will deliver two messages at next week's round-table meeting. In the first instance, she will tell industry leaders that they need to meet the moment, take responsibility and tackle issues of safeguarding on their own. But she will add that if their response is not good enough, the government might have to intervene.Intervention could include forcing participation in the CIISA.The culture secretary also said she recently appointed two "freelance champions in recognition of the fact that for freelancers in particular, there is a real problem in these industries." Multiple government ministers gave statements on Wednesday that called for further restrictions on the use of non-disclosure agreements (NDAs).Women and equalities minister Bridget Phillipson told Sky News that there was "scope to go further" on legislation that restricted the use of such agreements to ensure that the legal system was not being "abused in order to silence women"."We cannot have a system where rich and powerful individuals - rich and powerful men - are able to silence women and stop things coming to light," she said. Can't Buy My Silence founder Zelda Perkins told BBC Newsnight that there were "not enough safeguards" around high-profile people in creative industries and that joining the CIISA should be "mandatory".The former assistant to jailed film producer Harvey Weinstein broke an NDA in 2017 when she spoke publicly about the movie mogul's mistreatment of women.She has since founded a group that campaigns against NDAs being used in legal contracts or settlements to stop people from speaking out against their employers."There are no other regulatory bodies that are voluntary to join," Perkins told BBC Newsnight, referring to CIISA, noting that "obviously the people who need to be monitored are the people who are not joining"."It's still very wild west in the the creative industries, people behave how they want," she said, adding that while "you can't change the humans, you can change the rules around them".

schema.headline: Media industry could be forced by government to improve safeguards after David Walliams allegations

title: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry says
description: At least six people have been killed and about 20 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital, the biggest in the southern Gaza Strip, the Ham
body: At least six people have been killed and about 20 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital, the biggest in the southern Gaza Strip, the Hamas-run health ministry says.Eyewitnesses told the BBC that a single missile fired by a warplane hit a building containing the surgical wards and intensive care units overnight.The health ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were killed, among them surgeon Dr Rizk Abu Shaira. It condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions".The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who had used the hospital as a "headquarters" to plan attacks on its forces.Hamas said that Israel was spreading "false narratives" in a "blatant attempt to cover up a new war crime".Under international law, hospitals have a protected status, but they have been repeatedly targeted during the Gaza war.Israel accuses Hamas, which retains security control of parts of Gaza not occupied by Israeli troops, of cynically exploiting civilian infrastructure. It says the group stores weapons and runs command and control rooms in hospitals, which Hamas denies.Israel does not allow international news organisations, including the BBC, into Gaza, making it difficult to verify what is happening in the territory.In a video posted on social media, a paramedic from the Civil Defence agency who arrived at the building after the strike early on Thursday said the missile penetrated the five-storey structure and hit a room in the surgical department.A spokesman for the Civil Defence, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry, initially said that five people had been killed and 20 others injured.Videos shared by activists showed thick smoke inside the building and extensive destruction on the second floor, where medical equipment and beds had been scattered by the blast.Local activists have also circulated claims that the strike may have targeted a senior Hamas security figure who was hiding inside the building.Speaking to reporters in the aftermath of the strike, the director of Nasser hospital said the building had been hit in a vertical strike, causing extensive damage.Nasser hospital was hit by a double Israeli strike in August 2025, which killed at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers.Israeli strikes on Gaza have continued despite a ceasefire agreement in October last year.More than 1,620 people have been killed since then, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire.The humanitarian crisis in Gaza has recently worsened as a result of heavy rains that reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced families.The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

schema.headline: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry says

title: COP31: Burnham says climate consensus 'gone' but pledges 'new era of leadership'
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned that the consensus on both science and climate change has "gone".Addressing other world leaders and delegates a
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned that the consensus on both science and climate change has "gone".Addressing other world leaders and delegates at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, he said that despite this, the UK was ready to begin a "new era of British leadership" on the climate change issue.But environmental campaigners at the summit said the PM had to back up his warm words with stronger actions.In recent months, the UK government has announced policies which critics say have weakened its green credentials, such as reducing support for heat pumps, approving the Jackdaw gas field and doubling down on support for Heathrow Airport's expansion.Burnham opened his speech on Thursday by talking about the heat experienced in the UK this past summer.He said "it was not normal" - in fact it was the hottest on record, made 130 times more likely because of climate change, according to the Met Office.Hundreds of schools were closed, cereal harvests were down 11%, and ambulance services were inundated with calls beyond levels seen during the Covid-19 pandemic.As a result of the threat to people's health and homes, the PM said he was creating the UK, and the world's, first climate security envoy, Dame Madeleine Alessandri.Alessandri, the former head of the Joint Intelligence Committee, said: "Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates."As a result this was "placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world", she added.This will be seen as a strong indication of the focus of the UK's priorities when it takes up the G20 presidency next year. The current president is the US, which has been a notable absentee from the COP process over the last two years since President Trump withdrew the country from the most important global climate treaty - the Paris Climate Agreement.Professor Lord Nicholas Stern, who identified 20 years ago that climate change could cost the global economy up to 20% of GDP if left unchecked, praised the PM's words."The Prime Minister was right to identify climate change as a threat to security around the world, and the importance of investments in clean electricity generation as the best way of protecting households and businesses from the high prices and volatile markets for fossil fuels," he said.On tackling the causes of climate change, Burnham said his government remained committed to meeting the country's target of net zero by 2050 whilst also getting bills down.He said key to this was cutting our "dependence on fossil fuels" and increasing electrification - the amount of our energy needs met from renewable electricity.The main driver of rising global temperatures has been the increasing concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely caused by burning fossil fuels.Turkey, the co-hosts of COP31, wants a key outcomes of this year's summit to be a commitment by countries to meet 35% of their energy supply from electricity by 2035. Currently, it is around a fifth. But Burnham has been accused of having double standards."The Prime Minister simply cannot call for clean power across the world while saying yes to more fossil fuels in the UK," said Beth John, climate adviser at Oxfam.Last month, the government approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on the grounds that it provided energy security. And in the budget last month Chancellor John Healey announced a funding cut to the Warm Homes Plan, which provides grants and loans to support the installation of heat pumps.Whilst this week there has been media speculation that the government is considering watering down electric car sales targets, although the government insists no decision has been made.Successfully switching petrol and diesel cars to EVs and moving from gas boilers to electric-powered heat pumps are key ways to achieve the 35% electrification target, external.Although there was no royal presence this year, King Charles III sent a message ahead of Burnham's speech."As the world gathers for Cop31, I can only hope that this same spirit of partnership and common purpose can help inspire the collective action that our planet – and future generations – so urgently need."Our children and grandchildren will not judge us by the promises we made, but by what we chose to do."Burnham was the only G7 leader to speak at this year's conference in a sign of faltering support for the COP process - something he acknowledged in his speech.In an almost word for word copy of Sir Keir Starmer's address last year he said: "The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate has gone, and the reality is now the world will reach 1.5 degrees."Other leaders expected to speak on Thursday include many island states like Tonga, Tuvalu and the Solomon Islands.For these nations, the impact of climate change is already at their front door. With most of their land just metres above sea level, rising water levels have caused many to abandon their homes in recent years.Last year, Australia - the co-host of the COP31 summit - opened up the world's first climate visa for Tuvalu citizens wanting to evacuate.The first intake was massively oversubscribed, with more than a third of the population entering the ballot.As glaciers continue to melt and oceans expand, average sea levels are expected to keep climbing and potentially accelerate. The World Meteorological Organisation said on the opening day of this conference the global mean sea level was at its highest level since records began.

schema.headline: COP31: Burnham says climate consensus 'gone' but pledges 'new era of leadership'

title: Was Delhi pollution data during Diwali misleading?
description: Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesByShruti Menon and Barbara MetzlerBBC VerifyBBC Verify has found significant discrepancies between two I
body: Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesByShruti Menon and Barbara MetzlerBBC VerifyBBC Verify has found significant discrepancies between two Indian government datasets showing Delhi's air pollution during Diwali, indicating official figures may not have captured the full extent of the problem.As fireworks lit up Delhi's skies on 8 November to mark one of India's biggest festivals, some monitoring stations recorded very high levels of PM2.5, a fine particulate matter which can damage people's lungs and cause other serious health problems.But every hourly PM2.5 reading above 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre was missing from the widely cited air quality index (AQI) published by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), when compared to data from the Delhi Pollution Control Commission (DPCC).Delhi is one of the most polluted cities in the world and often has dangerously poor air quality, so it is vital people living in India's capital can trust the official data. Firecrackers are not the only cause of pollution, which is also attributed to a mix of reasons including vehicle emissions, construction dust, farm fires and atmospheric factors. But they can worsen air quality, especially in winter. Image source, ReutersThe CPCB, whose figures are generally cited by Indian media, has issued a statement which said readings above 1,000 micrograms are treated as "outside" the range for detection its equipment has been calibrated for and are excluded from calculations."During extreme episodes which are occasional like Diwali firecracker bursting, this may appear as a data gap at the particular station concerned, and those hours do not contribute to the 24-hour average of relevant pollutant for concerned station," the statement added.Dr Manoj Kumar, a researcher at Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), told BBC Verify that excluding high readings risks misrepresenting actual pollution levels and could cause people to lose trust in official figures.Our analysis found that, across the same 30 stations over 24 hours covering Diwali night, available CPCB readings averaged 240 micrograms per cubic metre - less than half the average of 551 in DPCC's data.What does the pollution data show?On the night of Diwali from Sunday into Monday, Delhi's already high pollution levels rose sharply as the celebrations peaked.Three different pollution monitoring stations recorded PM2.5 hourly concentrations above 3,000 micrograms, DPCC data examined by BBC Verify shows.Dr Kumar said that even a short-term exposure to extreme levels of particulate matter can have adverse health impacts.The World Health Organization's air quality guidelines state that annual average concentrations should not exceed five micrograms per cubic metre.Between 21:00 local time (15:30 GMT) on 8 November and 07:00 on 9 November, during the peak of Diwali celebrations, 217 hourly PM2.5 observations were missing across 59 CPCB monitoring stations in Delhi. Only 16 stations reported complete data during this period, while 43 had at least one missing observation.None of the 116 readings above 1,000 micrograms from the 30 DPCC-managed stations appeared in the CPCB's published records they feed data into.This matters because stations need at least 16 hours of valid PM2.5 measurements to calculate a daily average, according to CPCB's methodology. So a station with too many missing or invalid readings will not contribute to official pollution calculations.One example of a station with several hours of missing data was at RK Puram in south Delhi, where pollution peaked at nearly 2,500 micrograms.Using hourly PM2.5 readings from this station, BBC Verify calculated an average concentration of about 945 micrograms over the 24-hour period after 17:00 on 8 November.But similar averages of CPCB's published data for 14 of those 24 hours produced a much lower figure of 299 micrograms. The missing 10 hours also meant this data was not included in daily average calculations.The missing data across the city means that, despite a sharp overnight rise in pollution at some monitoring stations, CPCB reported Delhi's AQI at 344 at 16:00 on 9 November, down from 376 at the same time the day before.Dr Sierra Clark, an environmental epidemiologist from City St George's, University in London, warned classifying high pollution readings as missing could leave out days which "contribute the most to short-term health events, such as asthma attacks and heart attacks".She told BBC Verify "for transparency", Delhi's pollution reporting could show two scenarios including and excluding extreme pollution episodes."The latter would give a sense of typical pollution levels that are more representative of people's day-to-day experience. But it is also important to show the impact of those few days and what they contribute," Dr Clark added.Pollution in Delhi is not limited to PM2.5 and satellite imagery shows a thick haze over the city on 8 and 9 November.Satellite measurements of other pollutants like nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO) and fire activity in the atmosphere, rather than at ground level, showed increases on 8 November.But their overall average for Diwali week was not very high compared with 2024 and 2025.Graphics by Jess Carr and Tom Shiel.

schema.headline: Was Delhi pollution data during Diwali misleading?

title: 'You're triggering me': How to understand your therapy-speak teen
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByGeorge SandemanUpdated 1 hour agoWith claims of gaslighting, triggering and disrespecting boundaries, some parents are str
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByGeorge SandemanUpdated 1 hour agoWith claims of gaslighting, triggering and disrespecting boundaries, some parents are struggling to understand their teenagers' so-called therapy speak.When Carla Hoskins asks her 15 and 18-year-old sons to revise or do chores at their Hertfordshire home, she says she is sometimes met with: "You're triggering me!" Over in the US, Shannon Salvatoriello says her 14 and 17-year-old sons use similar words, which she says leaves her "feeling very confused". Mental health experts in the UK and US tell the BBC why young people are using terms often heard during therapy sessions in everyday conversation - and give parents tips on how to better understand their teenagers.  Image source, @carla_elizabeth87Image caption, Carla says she had never heard of terms like "triggering" or "gaslighting" before her teenage sons started using themMum-of-six Carla says she is sometimes accused of gaslighting by her teen sons - particularly when she asks about friends or schoolwork."I feel like any time you challenge them or request something is when you come up against this new language," says the 39-year-old."Rather than just saying, 'Mum, I'm stressed about my exams' or 'I've got a lot on my plate', it's I'm triggering them." She adds: "You can't really ever get to the bottom of anything."Carla says she had never heard the words triggering or gaslighting before her sons started using them and assumes they learned them on social media.New York psychiatrist Dr Suzanne Garfinkle-Crowell agrees this is one of the ways therapy speak has spread to everyday language. Social media is one of the places teenagers look to as they try to make sense of themselves and the world, she says.Image source, Dr Suzanne Garfinkle-CrowellImage caption, Dr Suzanne Garfinkle-Crowell says parents shouldn't argue with their children about the terms they useShe has observed a shift in the way young people talk about their problems - from describing their feelings to giving them labels, she tells BBC Radio 4’s Woman’s Hour."They would say, 'I'm not getting along with my mum'... 'School has gotten really challenging and I'm feeling kind of bad about myself', and then suddenly it was, 'I have attachment issues, ADHD, and depression'."Garfinkle-Crowell says parents shouldn't be afraid to consult a mental health professional if their child is describing symptoms of a medical condition, like anxiety disorder or depression.She understands that some parents feel the use of therapy speak by teens is "almost like they are speaking a new language", but says it is important they consider the backdrop to why they might be using it.Many young people, and girls in particular, often feel they aren't taken seriously by their parents and society more generally, she says."The only way to feel heard is to reach for this elevated medical language."The head of an independent review into youth mental health told BBC News in September it was "harder to be young" now. Prof Peter Fonagy said there had been a real rise in mental distress among young people given the economic and employment uncertainty their generation faces.Image source, The Samuel Therapy PracticeImage caption, Julia Samuel suggests using ordinary language to help build a connection with your childHowever, Julia Samuel, a psychotherapist from London, warns young people using medical terms such as anxiety disorder to describe "normal feelings like mild distress" can create a pattern of behaviour and emotions that result in them developing a disorder."It can give them the very thing they don't want," she explains. "It's the lack of knowledge and the overuse of the terms that can actually harm young people."Samuel says for parents struggling to understand therapy speak, "listening is your biggest tool to bridge the divide".She then suggests using "ordinary emotional language to reflect back" what your teenager is saying to help you understand what they are feeling.Woman's Hour - Therapy SpeakPsychiatrist Dr Suzanne Garfinkle-Crowell joins Nuala McGovern to discuss her concerns about the growing use of therapy speak and self-diagnosis.The interview about therapy speak starts at 17:05Garfinkle-Crowell agrees a helpful technique for parents is to think about the words you would associate with the therapy term a teen is using."You may try offering [something] like, 'That sounds like it could be really lonely for you. Is that part of it?'" she says.Mum-of-four Shannon, from New Jersey, says it took her several years to learn her approach of "I'm your parent and I'm asking you a question and you are going to answer me" was not helpful for her teenagers.She became frustrated when they would push back - sometimes using phrases about her not respecting their boundaries.Image source, @shannons_editImage caption, Shannon's children often tell her she's triggered them when she asks them about school or friendsSamuel says rather than asking teenagers questions in a direct manner, you could try talking about your own experience of a similar situation."You could bring up a subject about yourself at school or something that's related... so it isn't kind of pointing a finger at them," she says. Shannon says: "I've noticed when I do back off they will then come to me later to say, 'Hey, guess what? I got a 95 on that Spanish test'... You don't have to ask them for three days straight about something."Carla is glad she's open with her teenagers and feels they can discuss things with her - even if she sometimes struggles with the meaning."We are close and I think that's why sometimes they think that they can use these [therapy] words, as if they're talking to a friend."If you or someone you know is experiencing mental or emotional distress, you can access support from the BBC Action Line.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: 'You're triggering me': How to understand your therapy-speak teen

title: Andy Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in Labour and among other parties
description: There is renewed attention on the prime minister's push for closer relations with Europe - and that is causing ripples in his own party and others.And
body: There is renewed attention on the prime minister's push for closer relations with Europe - and that is causing ripples in his own party and others.Andy Burnham told his Cabinet earlier this week: "I firmly believe we have ended up with a harder Brexit than people voted for… no sensible person thinks the deal negotiated by the Tories is working for the country."It comes ahead of a week which will focus minds on the UK's relationship with the bloc. On Thursday, at a gathering of European leaders in Dublin, Burnham will for the first time meet those who could prove pivotal as he sells his vision for Britain's future in the bloc.And next week, he will deliver a speech on foreign policy, in which – for Burnham – Europe is a central plank. He will then travel to Brussels for a UK-EU summit to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility.Talking about the new deal to be signed at the summit, Burnham said to ministers: "We will take opportunities that make people in this country better off. "There is a significant prize."This lies behind the prime minister's decision to open the door to the argument about rejoining the EU single market - along with the freedom of movement that would bring - and even the EU altogether.But that longer-term ambition is dividing his cabinet and his party. Some welcome his approach, including those with formerly Brexit-backing constituencies. Angela Rayner, for example, is understood to have been pushing former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer to be bolder on Brexit since at least autumn 2022.The housing secretary is said to have been insistent that Labour needs to stick to its manifesto red lines – not to return to the EU single market, customs union, or freedom of movement – but is open minded to changing those at the next election.Another cabinet minister said: "The best thing you can do in politics is tell the truth. And the truth is that Brexit has been hugely damaging to Britain. "We are not leading a public conversation here, we are racing to catch up with the public."But others are watching nervously at a strategy one former minister described as "high risk".Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, for example, has struck a more cautious tone warning about the "costs and consequences" of rejoining the EU as well as staying out.Jonathan Reynolds, the Business and Trade Secretary, is supportive of getting closer to the EU and discussing the UK's long term relationship. But he has previously warned against joining the EU's customs union and is also unsure about the prospect of rejoining the EU, highlighting the uncertainty of what terms the UK would face, and what the bloc could look like in years to come with nationalist parties in the ascendancy in several European countries.A voice from the past has a different set of concerns. Lord Cameron told Bloomberg's Mishal Husain that starting a conversation about rejoining would be "very long and painful". The former prime minister warned "flirting with rejoining" could also harm Burnham's attempts to renegotiate the Conservative's Brexit deal."If you start endlessly producing this idea that we're actually on a path to rejoining, I think you're in danger of getting a less good partnership deal because of course the EU countries will just think: 'Well, these guys are gonna rejoin anyway, so what's the point in giving them a good partnership deal'."Attitudes in Labour towards the prime minister's approach don't divide along predictable lines. One Scottish Labour MP, personally opposed to Brexit and with a heavily Remain-voting constituency, said it was a "real problem"."How can I argue to my constituents that we had a Scottish referendum in 2014 that settled independence for a generation. but then say the 2016 referendum isn't settled? My view is you accept democracy."For now though, that opposition hasn't broken out into public rebellion, although Labour MP Gareth Snell is one who has warned about reopening the debate.The MP for Stoke-on-Trent, where the Leave vote was 69.4%, told the BBC's Westminster Hour that doing so would "monopolise an awful lot of time inside parliament, inside government" when there are other things MPs should be doing.Two Labour MPs among those most unhappy about Burnham's openness to Europe insisted "there are no plans" for any organised criticism of the prime minister.Despite their concerns, particularly about free movement, they described their current mindset as "wait and see". That temporary truce is likely to fracture if the prime minister's lead in the polls begins to slide.But Burnham's strategy has left other parties struggling to react.The Conservatives have strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules into the future, with the party leader Kemi Badenoch saying that would be a red line and "actually take us backwards".But some Conservative MPs are beginning to express unease about the strategic dilemma presented for their party by Burnham's moves on Europe, fearing that the issue could again divide Conservative voters.In recent months Badenoch and her team have intensified efforts to win back affluent voters, especially in the south of England, who view Burnham's economic offer as too left-wing."The problem is that some of those voters are only just giving us a hearing again after Brexit," one Conservative MP said, "and now they are going to keep being reminded of it."The Liberal Democrats have enjoyed being the most pro-European of the largest parties in Westminster. But some Lib Dems now fear their distinct position risks being drowned out by Burnham.Reform UK though say they are "very bullish" about the return of Brexit to political debate, despite polling that suggests public sentiment has shifted since 2016."If he [Burnham] wants to fight an election on a £40bn bill to rejoin, open door immigration, and less control over our laws and our courts then we are very up for that," a Reform UK strategist said. The party believes that just as it would build a progressive anti-Brexit coalition around Labour, it would also unite Brexit supporters around Reform UK as the most anti-EU party.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in Labour and among other parties

title: Daniel Thomas admits criminal damage of boat in English Channel
description: Activist Daniel Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, has admitted criminal damage after slashing a migrant dinghy with a knife in the English Channel.Th
body: Activist Daniel Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, has admitted criminal damage after slashing a migrant dinghy with a knife in the English Channel.The 37-year-old changed his plea to the single charge when he appeared via video link from prison at Portsmouth Crown Court on Thursday.A court previously heard that he had taken a boat into the English Channel and observed the migrant occupants of a dinghy being assisted by the RNLI lifeboat charity, Border Force and the French Coastguard.Thomas, whose address was withheld by the court at a previous hearing, admitted using a knife on the dinghy which had French personnel on board. He will be sentenced at the same court on 18 November.Prosecutor Kevin Lucie told Basingstoke Magistrates' Court in September the defendant instructed his boat be steered towards the empty rigid inflatable boat (RIB) that was adrift and then armed himself with a knife as rescue crews also approached the dinghy and a Frenchman boarded from a rescue vessel.After slashing the boat with the knife, Thomas could be heard on a livestream saying: "This is what needs to happen to everyone in these boats. Right, you're on English territory, This is England, this is not France anymore."Get off the boat, you have time to get off the boat. This is not France. Take them back."After he pleaded guilty to the charge of criminal damage at the magistrates hearing on Thursday, Thomas reiterated his plea of not guilty to failing to disclose the pin to his phone to police.

schema.headline: Daniel Thomas admits criminal damage of boat in English Channel

title: UFC: Usman Nurmagomedov slaps Merab Dvalishvili to spark mass brawl in Abu Dhabi
description: Dvalishvili called Nurmagomedov's older brother, Umar, "spoiled" before beating him in a bantamweight title fight in 2025.Umar Nurmagomedov is due to
body: Dvalishvili called Nurmagomedov's older brother, Umar, "spoiled" before beating him in a bantamweight title fight in 2025.Umar Nurmagomedov is due to take on American Urijah Faber at Saturday's event.There was previously an altercation between the two camps before the RAF event in July.UFC champion Islam Makhachev, who is a close friend and training partner of the Nurmagomedovs, suggested that incident led to Wednesday's altercation."Why were you silent when Merab hit a Dagestani wrestler for nothing and hurt his honor?" Makhachev wrote. "Merab started what happened today in his homeland by allowing himself to hit a guest and insulting his mother."Two-weight UFC champion Ilia Topuria, a friend of Dvalishvili, shared the footage of the incident on X and wrote: "Usman has reportedly been detained, along with the cowards who were with him."What a disgrace. A bunch of absolute cowards. I always thought you were a bunch of mediocre individuals. Now you've removed every last doubt."Honour, respect, and humility aren't words you preach. They're values you live by. And you've shown none of them."Nurmagomedov is a free agent after his last fight with the PFL and has been heavily linked with a switch to the UFC.MMA fighters often compete in RAF events alongside their careers in bigger promotions, with the likes of Khamzat Chimaev, Arman Tsarukyan and Colby Covington all recently appearing in the promotion.

schema.headline: UFC: Usman Nurmagomedov slaps Merab Dvalishvili to spark mass brawl in Abu Dhabi

title: Ukraine's power supply close to critical as Russian strikes bring darkness and cold
description: Daryna Kulchytska is a mum under pressure. A single parent in a seventh floor flat in Kyiv trying to feed two lively kids and ensure they do their hom
body: Daryna Kulchytska is a mum under pressure. A single parent in a seventh floor flat in Kyiv trying to feed two lively kids and ensure they do their homework. But Daryna also faces the added strain of a deadline she can't even be certain of.All she knows is soon the lights will go out, the sockets will lose power, the wi-fi will drop, and the taps will run dry. Tonight, the electricity has kept flowing an hour longer than advertised, but Daryna's still racing to serve dinner and finish her own work from home."The last few days it was only four or five hours we had power, but it's not at the same times. For two hours we have electricity, then for eight hours we don't."As peace talks continue, with US envoys meeting the Russian and Ukrainian leaders on Thursday, Ukrainians are facing a rolling schedule of planned power cuts because of intensified Russian attacks on their energy grid. Ukraine has responded by striking Russian oil refineries.Officials are concerned that life will quickly become unsustainable for millions of Ukrainians if power supplies cannot be maintained for at least four hours per day. Some privately warn that's close already, as some families are living with outages of up to 20 hours in Kyiv.The power cuts were introduced earlier this year than last winter, and they're already lasting longer - making homes like Daryna's darker and colder. She's wrapped in layers of clothing and a heavy coat - the temperature is dropping, indoors and out.Just before 7:30pm, there's a click and that's it - darkness until dawn. The lift doesn't work, the water will stop flowing because electricity is needed to pump it to their flat. So the torches and LED candles come out and Daryna, her son Kyryll and daughter Olena gather for a card game of Uno before an early night.Twelve-year-old Kyryll, speaking perfect English learned during two years living in the US, is frank about the disruption."There's no light, no water, no heat, no electricity. And no fun. All the fun got sucked out with the electricity," he says. "We have a lot of board games. We have a whole shelf, but we've played them like a hundred thousand times already."Many families sit in the shadows as blackouts sweep entire neighbourhoods, smothering homes and streets in darkness."You look outside and sometimes you see nothing. You have a big city around but you see nothing because there's no light," Daryna says.Kyiv has been worst hit - its metro trains and trolleybuses at times brought to a standstill. Nationwide, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians have gone without power in recent weeks.We saw why on a visit to one of Ukraine's largest power stations, barely standing after a recent ballistic missile strike - the most powerful and devastating attack of Russia's campaign against Ukrainian energy targets.The enormous plant - which we've been asked not to name for security reasons - has been reduced to a pile of twisted metal and broken pipes, its turbines buried in rubble, taking the site completely off line.Volodymyr Kovalenko was on duty in the control room keeping the plant working when the missiles hit at 3am."It was a very powerful attack. We'd never experienced anything like it. We'd had strikes before – part of the roof had collapsed, it was pretty grim. But this time it was particularly severe."Kovalenko, who followed in his parents' footsteps and has worked at the site for 25 years, says the damage is heartbreaking, though he's confident it can be repaired.But the work is being hampered by air raids every 15-30 minutes – seven times during our four-hour visit. Each warning of drones and further missiles forces teams to down tools and dive for cover, though during our visit all were shot down or flew on towards other targets.If there isn't time to reach the site's main shelter, the workers hide in the foundations of its towering chimneys."It's very difficult," says Vadym Bobyr, who is leading the recovery effort. "You've mentally prepared yourself to do a particular job, and then… the air raid siren goes off, and you have to get out as quickly as possible."The 39-year-old, who has worked here half his life, is dwarfed by the mangled ruins and daunted by the challenge of rebuilding the plant."It's emotionally difficult, because we've already repaired all this, got it running again, and now it's happened all over again. It hurts, but we keep working and getting things done."As we speak there's another alert - an incoming Banderol cruise missile. The workers dart through the maze of passages and pipework but there isn't time to reach a shelter - one of the plant's thickest walls will have to do for cover. The missile was eventually intercepted 5km (3 miles) away.Energy workers are at enormous risk. Since August there have been almost daily attacks on power facilities, claiming several lives every week. And it's getting more dangerous.On the edge of the site, with the latest threat over, a team returns to reinstating the power lines feeding the national grid. But they won't be carrying electricity from the shattered plant before the end of this winter, at least.President Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukraine still has enough generating capacity to meet electricity demand - the problem is getting it to homes and businesses when so many power lines and substations have been hit. Russia is using "waiter drones" that cling to pylons and cables and go undetected until Russia decides to detonate them.Maxim Timchenko, CEO of DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company, said Russia was already putting the degraded electricity grid under even greater pressure than last year, and that overstretched air defences were unable to protect all of Ukraine's critical infrastructure."What is different is the scale of attacks and the different types of weapons used in these attacks. This is what is the difference - they've doubled in power and in scale".He said rebuilding the damaged power station would take at least until next summer, because workers under sustained attack were limited to only one or two productive hours per day."We are fighting for survival of not only the whole country but ordinary people, especially during winter," Timchenko says.Kovalenko echoes the sense of mission about trying to keep the lights on. "Energy is the foundation of everything - people's lives, the state. Nothing can function without it. I've dedicated my entire life to this".Many are choosing to leave the capital, or Ukraine altogether, to avoid months of bitter cold. Daryna, Kyryll and Olena know the winter has barely begun."It's the worst feeling," Kyryll says. "When I get home from school, I'm tired. I lay in my bed. Bam! Air alarm. Bam! No lights. Bam! A lot of homework. Bam!"When the children are in bed Daryna confides her thoughts of moving to somewhere safer, or warmer. She's torn by the desire to stay at home - close to friends and relatives - and the worry of how unbearable life may become.The strain is damaging her mental health, she tells me, and she fears the impact on Kyryll and Olena, who suffers nightmares. Still, Daryna remains defiant despite the darkness."I don't want to live without light. But actually people in Ukraine say, OK, without light, but without Russians. Yes, we're scared, we're scared a lot. But better for us to be without power, but [also] without Russians."Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko, Kamila Hrabchuk and Daniel Wittenberg

schema.headline: Ukraine's power supply close to critical as Russian strikes bring darkness and cold

title: English councils displaying only one in 20 publicly owned artworks
description: How much art does your council own and is it locked away or on display?Image source, Rugby Borough CouncilImage caption, Councils across England own h
body: How much art does your council own and is it locked away or on display?Image source, Rugby Borough CouncilImage caption, Councils across England own hundreds of thousands artworks, but what are they doing with it all?ByEma SabljakEngland Data UnitFewer than one in 20 artworks owned by English councils are on public display, the BBC has found.More than 500,000 pieces of art are held in the collections of 225 councils, but the vast majority is being kept in storage.Local authorities remain "the biggest single constituent of public funding for arts and culture", according to the chief executive of the charity Art UK.Yet many face a strain on storage space and resources, with a real-term fall in spending for museums leading to challenges in displaying council-owned art.Council art collections include works by notable artists like Tracey Emin, David Hockney, LS Lowry and Antony Gormley.Some of those collections include tens of thousands of pieces, with the largest collection of 125,000 works belonging to Waltham Forest Council.Only a fraction of councils were able to provide the value of the collection but even individual collections had insurance values worth millions of pounds.As of April, just 26,856 of more than half a million works were being displayed by the 225 councils who shared data with the BBC. But what options do these local authorities have?Show itOnly one responding authority with more than 100 pieces of art - Rugby Council in Warwickshire - had them all on display.All of its 257 artworks were exhibited together for the first time in April.Sally Godden, manager of Rugby Art Gallery and Museum, said art had the power to connect communities."If things have been squirrelled away, then it's not going to do that," she said."It's not just a picture on the wall. It's how it connects to somebody and makes people think."Image source, Rugby Borough CouncilImage caption, Sally Godden said the museum team aimed to ensure the council collection instilled "pride in the people of Rugby"Godden said: "We can have the best collection in the world, but if they're not accessed, if they're not seen, if they're not enjoyed, if they don't make people think, then what's the point of them? They are so much more than an asset."We are very lucky to have such a great collection and continue to collect as well. By continuing to do that, we're growing stories, we're growing the diversity of the town, we're growing the views of people."The council has backed a funding bid for the redevelopment of Rugby Art Gallery and a museum which would include a permanent space to display the council-owned collection.Sell it?Many of the council art collections are still growing and only 10 councils actively disposed of any of the art they own during the past six financial years.Derbyshire sold 356 artworks in 2021-22, while North Lincolnshire sold 22 at auction in 2023-24.The other eight councils said the items moved out of their collections had been donated, transferred to other museums, or disposed of. For Derbyshire, the sale came as part of the closure of its Schools Library Service which had loaned art to schools. When the service was closed after 72 years, the council did not have the space or staff to keep the collection.Image source, Rugby Borough CouncilImage caption, Rugby, which is among the councils adding to their collections, recently acquired a painting selected by students and pupils living in the townKent did not respond to the question, but previously confirmed to the BBC it had sold 418 artworks in the 12 months to April. At the time, councillor Paul Webb said: "The reason for selling is a practical one, with the closure of the basement store where the art works are kept."I am sure the works have brought a lot of joy over the years to many people, and will now continue to do so."The council also recently sold a sculpture back to Gormley, the artist who created the Angel of the North.The chief executive of Art UK, Andew Elis, said that if all councils were to sell off art, our lives would be stripped of "these extraordinary artworks that should be there to enrich and engage us and brighten up our lives".Scan itArt UK has spent years photographing public art collections to create a digital record of more than one million artworks, external. Ellis said it was "really important" to give communities access to publicly owned art."We own in the UK arguably the greatest public collection of art in the world," he said. "Art changes lives, it enriches lives, it enriches our sense of place."The beauty of bringing all this together on one platform is that you make this art available for everyone, everywhere, all the time."From our point of view, this is not just about getting the art up online, this is about telling the stories behind the art and giving people agency over it." He added councils should make more use of the shared resource, especially with increased strain on finances.Councillor Mick Barton, who chairs the Local Government Association's culture committee, said communities should be able to enjoy local art and historic exhibits.But he said councils continued to face significant financial pressures which were leaving them with less money to provide "discretionary services, such as museums".Once adjusted for inflation, the net spend on museums across English councils has fallen by a fifth between 2017-18 and 2025-26. Store itKeeping the collections in storage does not always mean there is no access to the work.Three of the responding authorities that owned more than 100 artworks said none were on display.One of them, Rochdale Council in Greater Manchester, is not currently displaying any of its 1,701 artworks due to the regeneration of its Touchstones museum.Its temporary closure saw the entire collection moved into the council's stores, which had to be reorganised to accommodate the works.Senior curator Sarah Hodgkinson said they had been "taking a bit more risk than we have in the past" by bringing items from the collections directly to the public. That has seen a "lively" programme, including taking pieces to schools, picnics in the park or events.It has also let them catch up on the "behind-the-scenes" tasks of looking after a collection, like the storage and preservation.Image source, Your TrustImage caption, Mark Doyle said it was "fair to say that when we reopen, there will be more of the collections on display at any one time than there ever has been"Hodgkinson said: "We've taken loads of collections out into the community as part of our collections on tour programme."We've been working on repacking all of our sculpture collection, making sure our documentation is being worked on."Mark Doyle is director of arts, heritage and wellness at Your Trust, which delivers culture and leisure service on behalf of Rochdale Council."A lot of people don't understand what's involved in looking after a collection and making sure that it's there for future generations to be able to access and see," he said.Doyle said they often came across the "misconception" that the museum should have all of the items on display at the same time."Obviously that's not possible," he said. "But also there's other stuff that people don't understand about not having things on display for too long because it begins to deteriorate or they begin to be affected by the environment." Additional reporting by Lauren Woodhead and Jonathan Fagg.

schema.headline: English councils displaying only one in 20 publicly owned artworks

title: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
description: Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to under a radical overhaul of the welfare system to be recommended by a gove
body: Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to under a radical overhaul of the welfare system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review.As reported in the Times,, external Alan Milburn's year-long report, to be published on Tuesday, is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits.Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 16 to 24 year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet".He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants.His report is expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of universal credit or personal independence payment (Pip).Instead, they would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit.Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions.Some claimants would receive less under the plans - although the exact amounts will not be clear until early next year, when the government publishes legislation to implement the changes. People can claim Pip to help them with the additional cost of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions. It is available to those both in and out of work.Of the four million people claiming Pip in England and Wales, around 430,000 are aged between 16 and 24.In his interim report,, external Milburn said survey data found that 19% of young people claiming disability or health benefits were in work. Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers.Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate.Milburn told the Times: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system."But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances."I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around."Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets, data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year. Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare changes last year under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.Bell Ribeiro-Addy, one of the Labour backbenchers who revolted against Starmer's proposed reforms last year, said she was "not sure" she could vote to cut the benefit entitlement of existing claimants, adding that opposition to this idea had been a factor in last year's welfare rebellion."I don't think you get a disabled young person into work by taking away the money that helps them get into work," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme. A government spokesperson said: "We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work." The reforms would represent a radical overhaul of Britain's welfare system, at a time when there is heavy political pressure for the UK to find the money to spend more on defence.Both the Conservatives and Reform UK have argued for significant cuts to welfare, including to fund a boost to defence.If Milburn's recommendations were approved, it could take almost a decade for the British state to see monetary savings.The new system "will need significant investment" and would involve "rebuilding the system from scratch", Milburn said.His new proposed system would involve an element of carrot and stick, wherein young people could lose some of their benefits if they did not engage with the extra work support options.In an interview recorded on Tuesday, Skills Minister Jacqui Smith told the BBC that young people had a "responsibility" to take up employment support."It is a contract. People need the chance, and they need to take that chance," she added.A separate review - co-chaired by disabilities minister Sir Stephen Timms - examining disabilities benefits is also expected to be published this month.

schema.headline: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say

title: Ciara Oliva: Cyclist and mother-of-three on her Olympic dreams after Great Britain return
description: Dreaming of the Olympics is one thing.Getting yourself back on a world class programme, with a baby and two pre-schoolers to look after, was a differe
body: Dreaming of the Olympics is one thing.Getting yourself back on a world class programme, with a baby and two pre-schoolers to look after, was a different matter entirely.At that time, less than two years ago, Oliva says she told a few close friends and family that she was considering coming out of retirement."'Are you crazy?' was the reaction," she admited. "'Are you sure? You're sleep-deprived!'"But I think that they also know what I'm like and they also know how much the Olympics means to me."So to now make it back to the Great Britain Cycling Team is just the biggest honour. It is the biggest team effort from Lewis, my husband, who supports this 100% and [the children's] grandparents. I couldn't do it without them. "We had Lewis's parents out on a training camp with us in Italy so that we were able to train together."It really pushes me on."Just being back at the top table of British cycling is an impressive achievement, especially when you consider the strength of the current women's endurance programme.At last month's Track World Championships, Great Britain took gold in the women's team pursuit. Millie Couzens then led a GB one-two in the individual pursuit. Anna Morris ended the Championships with three golds.Oliva admits that getting final selection for the Los Angeles Games will be a 'tall order'.But then again, so was getting this far.With two children at school and a toddler at home, fitting in training is a challenge.She aims to do her indoor turbo sessions while her youngest naps. If not, they can often still be happening at ten o'clock at night.And in this second chapter of her career, Oliva is placing a lot more emphasis on strength work.She says she is targeting areas she would have described as weaknesses ten years ago and as a result she is faster and stronger than she has ever been.And thanks to her young family, she is certainly more motivated than ever."[My eldest daughter] is my biggest supporter," Oliva continued."Yesterday I had my GB suit out and she was holding it up with such pride. And I said to her, Mummy had to work really hard to get that back, you know. And she said I know, Mummy, I see it every day."Chase your dreams and don't be afraid to shout that out. Because it can seem scary. There's always the 'what if you don't make it?'"But then what if you do?"Oliva has ridden this path before. But never quite like this.And she is determined that, this time, her Olympic story has a happy ending.

schema.headline: Ciara Oliva: Cyclist and mother-of-three on her Olympic dreams after Great Britain return

title: King Charles appears on Sir Elton John's radio show
description: King Charles III has appeared on Sir Elton John's radio show in an episode set to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.During the Rocket Hour sho
body: King Charles III has appeared on Sir Elton John's radio show in an episode set to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.During the Rocket Hour show, the King said the pop star had become "a national treasure after all these years", to which the singer joked: "I'll be on the Antiques Roadshow.""Join the club," the King replied.The pair discussed some of their favourite musical performances, as well as the role music has played in the King's charity, the King's Trust. The show was recorded in secret last month and will air this Saturday.Sir Elton has long been a supporter of the trust, most recently donating a pair of his rose-tinted glasses to its 50th anniversary auction this year.In a trailer for the upcoming episode, the King and Sir Elton are seen laughing together as they chat.In a voiceover, the singer said he was "excited to hear what he's got to say about music, about the King's Trust and memories that we both share".The King's Trust - previously known as The Prince's Trust - was established by Charles in 1976 to help young people from disadvantaged backgrounds overcome challenging situations, become employed or launch their own businesses.During the radio episode, the King called it "an opportunity too good to resist" when he was asked to showcase music from the "talented performers who have so generously supported us over the years, together with some of the newer artists the trust has helped to launch".The full list of their chosen tracks is under wraps until the episode airs but Skye Newman's Hairdresser, Raye's Joy and Muse's rendition of Feeling Good are said to be among them.The pair will reminisce about some of the most memorable performances for the trust, from the Wembley Arena rock galas of the 1980s - which Sir Elton participated in - to charity shows at the Royal Albert Hall and pop concerts in Hyde Park.The episode was recorded at Apple Music Studios - which hosts the show - in Battersea Power Station when the King and Sir Elton visited for the launch of the Apple x King's Trust Creative Labs.The mentorship programme aims to help young people explore careers in creative industries.

schema.headline: King Charles appears on Sir Elton John's radio show

title: Andy Robertson set to make history but hero Kenny Dalglish will always be King
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Andy Robertson is one of two centurions for Scotland menByBBC Scotland's chief sports writerAndy Robertson sa
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Andy Robertson is one of two centurions for Scotland menByBBC Scotland's chief sports writerAndy Robertson says it gives him "goosebumps" any time he thinks about it. Friday at Hampden, North Macedonia the visitors, a 102nd cap to be won and, when it is, he'll be level in the pantheon with Sir Kenny Dalglish, the football man he loves more than any other.On Monday in St Gallen, Switzerland - all being well - Robertson will break the great man's record, a mark that has stood for 40 years.The Tottenham left-back is sitting in the boardroom at Queen's Park in the shadow of Hampden with a phone in his hand and eyes fixed on his 19-year-old self coming off the bench in Warsaw on 5 March, 2014."Nervous, excited, living the dream, not knowing what road I was on," he smiles as he looks at the moment he takes his first touch in international football. "As I was going on, Gordon [Strachan, Scotland manager] said to me, 'remember why you're here, play like you play at Dundee United, don't play safe'. The first ball, when it came to me, I just drove forward about 30, 40 yards."I had pretty much every emotion that day. My mum and dad were there. My brother. My aunt and uncle. My other uncle. There's a picture of me and my brother [Stephen] at the airport after the game. He had a big Poland hat on and a half-and-half scarf. He was well oiled by that point."Nations League: Scotland v North Macedonia13/11/26'I've never actually been confident'Robertson says he'd have laughed out loud had you told him then what lay ahead of him - two Premier Leagues, two League Cups, an FA Cup, a Champions League, a Super Cup, a Club World Cup, soon-to-be the most capped male Scottish players in history and, by a mile, the one with the most games as captain of the men's team."I've never actually been confident," he says, which is a surprise admission given everything he's done. Maybe what he means is that he always had a quiet belief in his own ability but found that constantly questioning himself was who he was and who maybe who he still is. "I've always doubted myself and that's always got the best out of me. I've always tried to prove people wrong and prove myself wrong. The one thing I didn't do was look too far ahead. I always just lived in the here and now and that's served me well."In the room where he's talking there are a dozen normal chairs and away to the side, detached from the rest, is an elaborate seat. A high-backed, ornate, somewhat regal affair.It looks fit for a king and, given the history Robertson's about to make, maybe he should plonk himself in it. And that brings us back to the man whose record he's about to match and surpass.  "There are normal seats but there's one throne and Kenny Dalglish should be sat on it," he says. "Friday night's not about me. Friday night's about the greatest player of all time in our country, and for me, that will always be Kenny.Figure caption, You've done Liverpool and Scotland proud - Kenny Dalglish on Andy Robertson's career"He's had this record for so long. He deserves it. If he played in a different era, he would probably have played a number of games that wouldn't have been able to be caught. "Sometimes - not as a criticism - as a country we're maybe not good at recognising how good people we've got are. For me, he's the best player to ever play with Scotland and arguably Britain. "We have to appreciate that man because I certainly do, my family certainly do and, I think on Friday, I'll have him at the front of my mind, the back of my mind and I'm not really bothered about myself."It's a lovely thing, that. Robertson, about to draw level with Dalglish, is only thinking about Dalglish. The depth of feeling comes tumbling out of him when he starts telling stories about what King Kenny means to his family and how he seemingly created a miracle by momentarily curing Robertson's beloved late grandfather's hearing."I always remember my agent talking to me about the first time he met Liverpool," Robertson says of a time when he was still with Hull but about to move to Anfield."He met the chief scout and sporting director and all of a sudden Kenny 'accidentally' walked into the room. It was 100% planned, I know it was planned. "One of the things right at the top of the list for me was the fact [by joining Liverpool] I got to meet Kenny in person and I've actually got to have a relationship with him and his family, because his family are special."My dad, in particular, has met people in football through me, but I've never seen him being starstruck by anyone apart from Kenny. "I always remember, we'd just beaten Barcelona 4-0 [in May, 2019] to qualify for my second Champions League final. My grandad was at the game and I managed to grab Kenny afterwards. I says, 'Kenny, would you mind coming in to see my grandad and my uncle? They would love to see you'. "Bear in mind his grandson's just qualified for another Champions League final and he basically barged me out of the way and shook Kenny's hand. "My grandad had hearing aids. He couldn't really hear much of us but he heard everything Kenny said, so it did open a lot of questions in the family as to how bad the ear problem was with my grandad. He's no longer with us but to see how happy he was… Kenny was his hero."'Person first, footballer second'When Robertson moved to Liverpool for the hilariously small sum of £8m in 2017, his wife, Rachel, was expecting their first child. The Dalglishes, he says, helped so much that he could hardly ever repay them for their support and friendship. On the pitch and off, the transfer to Liverpool as a 23-year-old was the greatest move he could have possibly made.In reflective mood, on the cusp of Scottish football history, Robertson talks about his mother and father and his brother. "They're as proud of my brother as they are of me," he said. "The exact same, whatever achievements we have. But I think they're more proud of the men we've become. That was always most important for me."Anyone who knows me, my family, my friends, I always want them to like the person first, the footballer second. Anyone that only wants to know me as the footballer, then I don't let them get too close but if they want to know me as the person first and foremost, then they're the people that are really in my close circle. "I've still got the same friends I went to nursery with at three years old. Three of my best friends."Robertson says he often thinks about the game in Scotland and whether young kids today are getting the kind of opportunities he got. "We talk about that - my story, John McGinn's story, Ryan Christie's story," Robertson said."There'll be a hundred people going, 'I could have been that'. Football has a lot to do with ability and mentality, but also you need a little bit of luck as well."It's about trying to protect the 15, 16, 17-year-olds just now and we all have a duty to help with that. We always want the young players to come in and I just love their energy, I love how excited they are. Findlay Curtis just bounces about all the time. "These are the kids that are going to bring the country forward. They're all sitting at the other end of the table playing games we don't even know about but it's great for us to sit back and go, 'OK, we're part of this squad, but when we leave, then hopefully Scotland will be in a good place."To Friday, then. A record-equaller but, to Robertson, this is no nostalgia trip. This is a game Scotland desperately want - and need - to win.He says they were a yard off it in all areas last time out against Slovenia. "Unacceptable," he recalled. "We didn't give our fans anything to shout about."He departs with fighting words about the desire within the squad to make amends. Out the door, down the corridor and onwards into history. Seconds later, he returns.  "Forgot my washbag," he laughed. "Bet Kenny didn't have one of these!"Glasgow, Liverpool, Scotland - the ties that bind.

schema.headline: Andy Robertson set to make history but hero Kenny Dalglish will always be King
